rv.q: But in fact, this is a ferociously good revival from Jamie Lloyd, that almost totally reclaims, reinvents and reinvigorates a play so engrimed in period camp that it can sometimes feel like a chore to even remember it exists.
It's superbly acted and ferociously gripping.
This is the Royal Court at its best, giving us an uncompromisingly honest account of multicultural modern Britain.
All this would make for a pretty bleak evening if the performances weren't so shiningly good, and Bhatti's writing so sharp and witty.
Michael Longhurst’s production is a raggedly brilliant evening largely but not wholly thanks to him.
This is both its strength and its weakness: she homes in on issues that are of real concern, but dramatically, it becomes a bit of a pile-up.
There are times when the rapid whacking at the very many multicultural ‘issues’ included makes it feel like a race-drama splat the rat.
It's a shame as the play really crackles in places.
It's impossible not to be floored by the sheer power of this playwright's gut-wrenching prose.
Family tragedy is emotionally powerful but incomplete and unsatisfying.

cn.t: Bhatti's provocative drama powerfully dissects race, class and prejudice in multicultural Britain through a party that unravels relationships. Critics praise its mordant humor and emotional impact, though some find its structural ambitions don't fully cohere.
